la:verb:exuo.gloss: to extract, take out, draw out, pull off
senses: to extract, take out, draw out, pull off
put off, away, or out; take or strip off or away; remove; free from; lay or set aside
la:verb:exuo.html:
ex-ŭo, ŭi, ūtum, 3, v. a.
ex and root av-, to go to, put on; Zend. avaiti, go into, ao-thra, shoe; Slav. and Lith. forms, v. Fick, Vergl. Wört. p. 17; cf. ind-uo
,
to draw out or off, to pull or strip off, put off, divest (class.; esp. freq. since the Aug. period).
Lit.: serpens exuit in spinis vestem,: manticam umero,; cf.: pharetram umero,: telum magno e vulnere,: ensem vaginā,: clipeum reduci,; cf.: vincula sibi,: jugum,to shake off,: alas,to lay aside,: Trojanos cestus,: setosa duris exuere pellibus membra,; cf.: magnos membrorum artus, magna ossa lacertosque Exuit,strips, bares,: aliquem veste,: palmas vinclis,: digitos,i. e. to strip of rings,: mensas,to uncover,: si ex his te laqueis exueris,: se jugo,. —In a Greek construction: unum exuta pedem vinclis,: cornua exuitur,.—Absol.: si non saltas, exue igitur (sc. pallam),. —
Transf., in gen., to strip, despoil, deprive of any thing: hostium copiis fusis armisque exutis,i. e. to be forced to throw off their arms and to flee,: hostem armis,fin.; ; : exuti prope omnes armis diffugere,; ; : impedimentis,; : castris,; ; ; : sedibus,: aliquem avitis bonis,; cf.: aliquem patrimonio,: montes,to strip, lay bare,: se agro paterno avitoque,: exuto Lepido, interfecto Antonio, stripped bare, i. e. without legions, without arms, etc., .—
Trop., to lay aside, cast off, divest one's self of any thing: humanitatem,; cf. : sapientia vanitatem exuit mentibus,: mentitum colorem,: silvestrem animum,: vultus severos,: feritatem,: mores antiquos,: virtutes,: fidem,: amicitiam,: tristitiam et arrogantiam et avaritiam,: jus fasque,: promissa,to break one's word,: pacta,: patriam, et saep.: hominem exuens ex homine,: magistrum,—*
With a subjectclause: mihi quidem ex animo exui non potest, esse deos,.—
Transf., to make void of, to free from: se omnibus vitiis,.

la:verb:exuro.html:
ex-ūro, ussi, ustum, 3, v. a.,
to burn out, burn up, consume (class.; syn.: incendo, accendo, inflammo, cremo).
Lit.: illic oculos exuram lampadibus ardentibus,; : fores,: domi suae vivus exustus est,: vicos complures,: classem Argivum,.—
Transf., to dry up: loca exusta solis ardoribus,: paludem,: lacus,: agrum,: res exustae torrentibus auris,: caseum (sol),: segetem,: aliquem (sitis),; : Pyrrhus Italiam bellis saevissimis exurens,laying waste, devastating,.—
Trop.
To set on fire, kindle, inflame: (Venus) volt exurere divos,; cf. —
To consume, destroy: aliis scelus exuritur igni,: exustus flos veteris ubertatis,dried up,.

senses: alternative form of exuviae (“that which has been taken off or sloughed off; spoils, clothes, booty”)
skin of a snake etc. sloughed off
remains (that which has been taken off)
la:noun:exuviae.html:
exŭvĭae, ārum, f.
exuo
,
that which is stripped, drawn or taken off from the body, clothing, equipments, arms, etc. (mostly poet.).
In gen.: induviae tuae atque uxoris exuviae,; so : pyram Erige et arma viri ... exuviasque omnes ... super imponant,; cf. : cum fulmine et sceptro exuviisque Jovis,; cf. Fest. S. V. TENSA, p. 365, 1 Müll.: EXVVIAS FECIT, i. q. funus fecit, Inscr. in Bull. dell' .—The skin of an animal; (coluber) positis novus exuviis,his slough,; of the lion's hide, ; the tiger's hide, ; the golden fleece, ; .—Comic.: bubulae,thongs of ox-hide,.—Hair: devotae flavi verticis exuviae,; .—
In partic., spoils stripped from an enemy, as arms, booty, etc. (syn.: praeda, spolia, manubiae): locus (i. e. Rostra) exuviis nauticis et classium spoliis ornatus, * : (Hector) exuvias indutus Achilli,: haec arma exuviasque viri tua quercus habebit,: hostiles,; cf. bellorum,.—*
Trop.: tu ornatus exuviis hujus, venis ad eum lacerandum,.

la:verb:exubero.gloss: to abound or flourish; be abundant or fruitful
senses: to abound or flourish; be abundant or fruitful
la:verb:exubero.html:
ex-ūbĕro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a.
(poet. and in post-Aug. prose).
Neutr., to come forth in abundance, to grow luxuriantly; to be abundant, to abound in.
Prop.: cujus corpus in tam immodicum modum luxuriasset exuberassetque,: alte spumis exuberat amnis,: (frus) mox increscens ad medium noctis exuberat,: pomis exuberat annus, —
Trop.: ex multa eruditione, ex pluribus artibus exundat et exuberat eloquentia,: lucrum,.—
Act., to make full or abundant: quae favorum ceras exuberant,: materia melior vindemiis exuberandis,.—Trop.: Scythae exuberant Persas,i. e. overwhelm by numbers of immigrants,.—P. a.: exuberans, ntis.
Superfluous: hoc exuberantis quasi operis, ut, etc.,.—
Extraordinary: pernicitas,. —Hence, adv.: exuberante, superfluously, .
la:verb:exubero.inflection: āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a.

la:verb:exulto.gloss: to spring vigorously, leap or jump up

la:verb:exundo.html:
ex-undo, āvi, 1, v. n. and a.
Neutr., to flow out or over, to overflow (poet. and in post-Aug. prose).
Lit.: fons,: per quos (rivos) exundat piscina,: trunco cruor exundat,.—
Transf.
To be washed up, thrown out by the waves: tura balsamaque vi tempestatum in adversa litora exundant,.—
To pour forth abundantly, to rush forth; to overflow with any thing: flammarum exundat torrens,; cf.: exundant diviso vertice flammae,: spiritus (morientis) exundans perflavit campum,: inde Medusaeis terram exundasse chelydris,: exundans ingenii fons,: exundat et exuberat eloquentia,: temperare iram; eoque detracto quod exundat, ad salutarem modum cogere, which superabounds, is in excess, Sen. de Ira, 1, 7.—*
Act., to pour forth abundantly: fumum,.

la:verb:exulo.gloss: to live in exile, be banished

la:verb:exulcero.gloss: to cause to suppurate or ulcerate
senses: to cause to suppurate or ulcerate
la:verb:exulcero.html:
ex-ulcĕro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.,
to make sore, to cause to suppurate or ulcerate (class.).
Lit.: pulices solent ea (sc. aures al.) exulcerare,: cutem,: ventrem,: vulvas,: stomachum,: cicatrices,: panos nondum exulceratos,.—Absol.: omnis agitatio exulcerat,.—
Trop., to make worse, to exasperate, aggravate (syn.: corrumpo, perturbo): ea, quae sanare nequeunt, exulcerant,: gratiam (opp. conciliare),: in rebus ab ipso rege clam exulceratis, : dolorem,: ut in exulcerato animo facile fictum crimen insideret,: ira exulcerati animi,.
